message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
The pilot gives Cabinet something we rarely have in local climate policy: a clear before-and-after comparison with the rest of the county acting as a benchmark. Installations in the pilot districts rose by 70% against 20% elsewhere, a gap that is far too large to be chance, and households themselves told us the top-up was important in their decision. That is strong evidence the grant works. The value-for-money case is equally robust. Using standard carbon savings per installation and a conservative 15-year life, the Council paid about £56 per tonne, less than half its own £120 appraisal threshold. We have deliberately kept the design the same as the pilot, same grant level, same eligibility, same payment route, so we are scaling something proven rather than experimenting. The risks around installer capacity and national policy are real but manageable, and we have mitigations for each. I am confident this is one of the most cost-effective climate measures available to the Council.
</author>

The review is to check that the recommendation is clear and the document is ready to go to the decision-makers.

<document>
Policy Brief: Extending the Heat Pump Top-Up Grant Countywide
Climate and Environment Team, Harnley County Council, June 2026

1. Recommendation
That Cabinet extend the £2,500 local top-up grant for domestic heat pumps, piloted in two districts in 2025, to the whole county from April 2027, with a budget of £2.5 million a year for an initial two years.

2. Background
Domestic heating accounts for around a quarter of the county's carbon emissions, and most homes are heated by gas or oil boilers. The national boiler upgrade grant covers part of the cost of a heat pump, but survey evidence shows the remaining upfront cost is still the main barrier for households, with typical net costs of £4,000 to £7,000 after the national grant.

In January 2025 the Council launched a local top-up of £2,500 per installation in Ashby and Coleton districts, paid on top of the national grant. The top-up was available to owner-occupiers only, with the installation carried out by an accredited installer. The pilot ran for the full calendar year.

3. Results
Table 1. Heat pump installations, by district group
District group | 2024 installations | 2025 installations | Change
Pilot districts (Ashby, Coleton) | 140 | 238 | +70%
Other five districts | 210 | 252 | +20%
County total | 350 | 490 | +40%

Installations in the pilot districts grew by 70%, compared with 20% elsewhere. The top-up therefore caused around 50 percentage points of additional growth, and we expect a similar uplift in the remaining districts once the top-up is available countywide.

The pilot also had broader benefits. In March 2025 the regional installer training centre opened at Coleton College, and the number of accredited installers based in the two pilot districts rose from 9 to 23 over the year. Installers reported that the top-up gave them the confidence to recruit. Wait times for an installation survey in the pilot districts fell from around ten weeks to four.

Customer feedback was positive: of 196 households who completed the follow-up survey, 88% were satisfied or very satisfied with their heat pump, and 91% said the top-up was important in their decision.

4. Value for money
Grant payments in the pilot totalled £595,000 (238 installations at £2,500). Each heat pump replacing a gas or oil boiler saves about 2.1 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, so the 238 installations will save around 500 tonnes a year, or 7,500 tonnes over a 15-year equipment life. That is a cost to the Council of about £56 per tonne, well below the £120 per tonne threshold the Council uses to appraise climate investments.

5. Proposal
We propose a countywide top-up of £2,500 per installation, with the same eligibility and installer requirements as the pilot, capped at 1,000 grants a year (£2.5 million). On current trends, demand is likely to reach this cap in the first year. Because the pilot was open to landlords as well as owner-occupiers, we expect demand from the private rented sector to remain a significant share of applications, which supports the Council's private-sector housing standards objectives.

Administration would continue to be handled by the existing two-person grants team, with one additional post funded separately from the Council's climate reserve. Grants would be paid directly to installers on completion, as in the pilot, to reduce the risk of fraud.

6. Risks
Installer capacity outside the pilot districts is lower, and waiting lists could lengthen if demand rises sharply. We will work with the training centre to promote accreditation in other districts.
If the national grant is reduced, the local top-up may be insufficient on its own to sustain demand. We will review the scheme annually.

7. Conclusion
The pilot shows that a modest local top-up substantially increases heat pump uptake, at a cost per tonne of carbon well within the Council's threshold. Extending it countywide is a cost-effective way to accelerate the decarbonisation of home heating.
</document>
response:
# Review: Heat Pump Top-Up Grant brief

**Verdict: not ready to go to Cabinet.** The recommendation itself is clear and well-formed. But the value-for-money figure is miscalculated, the headline effect is overstated, and the brief contradicts itself on eligibility. The author's summary is also stronger than the document supports. Fixing these could change the conclusion, so I'd hold it until they're resolved.

## Must fix

**1. The £56/tonne figure doesn't follow from the brief's own numbers.**
£595,000 ÷ 7,500 tonnes is about **£79/tonne**, not £56. It is still under £120, but it is not "less than half" the threshold.

**2. Cost per tonne counts all 238 installations, but only the additional ones are attributable to the grant.**
By the brief's own comparison, the pilot districts would have reached about 168 installations at the 20% background growth (140 × 1.2). That implies about 70 additional installations, with the other 168 being grants paid for installs that would probably have happened anyway.
- 70 × 2.1 t × 15 years ≈ 2,205 tonnes
- £595,000 ÷ 2,205 ≈ **£270/tonne**, more than twice the £120 threshold
- To get under £120, roughly 157 of the 238 grants (about two-thirds) would need to be additional. The pilot suggests about 29%.

Even the corrected £79 is not the right number to show Cabinet. The brief should present the additionality-adjusted figure, with sensitivity ranges. It should also state whether admin costs and the extra post are included, and whether carbon savings assume a constant grid over 15 years. Savings from replacing gas and from replacing oil also differ.

**3. The uplift is confounded by the training centre.**
The Coleton College training centre opened in March 2025, in a pilot district. Accredited installers rose from 9 to 23 and survey waits fell from ten weeks to four. More supply and shorter waits could drive installations up independently of the grant. The brief mentions this as a "broader benefit" but then credits the whole 50-point gap to the top-up ("The top-up therefore caused…"). Either the effect should be described as top-up plus installer capacity, or the brief needs evidence to separate them. For example, it could compare Ashby with Coleton, or look at monthly trends before and after March.

This also undermines the forecast. The brief says capacity is lower in the other five districts, so the pilot uplift is unlikely to repeat there. "A similar uplift" is not supported.

**4. Eligibility contradicts itself.**
Section 2 says the pilot was for **owner-occupiers only**. Section 5 says it was **open to landlords as well**, and builds an argument about private rented demand on that. The proposal says "same eligibility as the pilot," so Cabinet can't tell what it is approving. This needs checking against the pilot rules and correcting, along with the private-sector housing claim if it falls away.

**5. The "demand will reach the cap" claim is unsupported.**
1,000 grants would be roughly double the county's *total* 2025 installations (490). Even at the pilot's +70% growth, the county would reach about 830 installs, and not all would claim a grant. Either show the demand modelling or soften this. It matters because the £2.5m ask rests on it.

## Should fix

- **Survey evidence is weak on causation.** The 91% "top-up was important" figure comes from grant recipients (196 of 238), and people who got a grant tend to say it mattered. It says nothing about households who would have installed anyway. Present it as supporting colour rather than evidence of effect. The 88% satisfaction figure is irrelevant to whether the grant works.
- **"Too large to be chance" misses the point.** Chance is not the main concern. Confounding and non-random district selection are. The brief doesn't say how Ashby and Coleton were chosen, or whether they differed from the others at the start.
- **Admin capacity.** A two-person team that handled 238 grants is being asked to handle up to 1,000, with one extra post. State whether that is enough.
- **Risks are thin.** Each has one line of mitigation ("promote accreditation," "review annually"). Installer capacity is central to whether the policy works, so it needs concrete actions, such as funding for training places outside Coleton, and a trigger for pausing or adjusting the scheme. Saying the risks are "manageable, with mitigations" overstates what's written.
- **Recommendation completeness.** Add the extra post and its reserve funding to the recommendation, since Cabinet is effectively approving it. Consider adding the review point and what would trigger a change at the two-year mark.
- **Update the data.** The brief is dated June 2026 and covers 2025 only. If 2026 pilot or county data exist, they would be a useful second look at the effect.

## Where the author's summary goes beyond the document

| Author says | Document supports |
|---|---|
| Gap "far too large to be chance" | Gap is real, but attribution to the grant is confounded |
| "Strong evidence the grant works" | Suggestive at best; installer capacity is an equal candidate |
| £56/t, "less than half" the threshold | £79/t on all grants; about £270/t on additional ones |
| "Scaling something proven" | Design is the same, but the eligibility description is inconsistent and the conditions (installer supply) differ outside the pilot |
| Mitigations exist for each risk | One sentence each |

## Suggested path

Recompute cost per tonne with additionality, resolve the eligibility discrepancy, and reframe the effect as grant plus capacity. The recommendation may still hold: the case might rest on a lower but real effect, or on a smaller or phased rollout paired with installer training. But it should be argued honestly, because on the current numbers the £120 test could well fail. If useful, I can draft the revised Section 3 and 4 wording or a sensitivity table.
